title: What HFT Is & How It Makes Money
tagline: Strip away the mystique: HFT is automated market participation where speed is the edge.

concept.analogy: Imagine a currency-exchange kiosk at an airport. It quotes a price to buy dollars and a slightly higher price to sell them, and it pockets the small difference on every transaction. It doesn't care which way the dollar moves long-term — it just wants to do millions of these tiny round-trips while never holding a big risky pile of cash. An HFT market maker is that kiosk, except the spread is a fraction of a cent, the transactions happen in microseconds, and a computer runs it.
paragraphs: High-frequency trading (HFT) is a subset of algorithmic trading defined by very high speeds, very high turnover (lots of orders), and very short holding periods — often milliseconds to seconds. Positions at the end of the day are usually small or flat. The 'edge' is not a deep view on where a stock will be in a year; it is being faster, smarter, and better-organized than other participants over tiny time windows.

HFT firms make money in a few repeatable ways. (1) Market making: continuously quoting a bid and an ask and capturing the spread plus, often, exchange rebates, while managing the risk of being 'run over' by informed traders. (2) Arbitrage: spotting the same or related instruments priced inconsistently across venues (e.g., an ETF vs. its underlying basket, or a future vs. spot) and trading them back to fair value. (3) Short-horizon statistical prediction: using signals like order-flow imbalance to predict the next tiny price move and trading ahead of it.

Because the edge is small per trade, two things matter enormously: scale (do it a huge number of times) and risk control (one bug or one bad fill repeated a million times is catastrophic). This is why HFT is as much a systems-engineering and risk-management discipline as it is a trading one — and why firms hire deeply technical people.

A crucial myth to drop: HFT is not 'predicting the market' in the Hollywood sense. Most HFT strategies are agnostic to long-term direction. They are closer to running a very efficient, very fast logistics operation on a flow of orders.
points: Speed is a means, not the product — the product is liquidity provision and price-correction, sold for a tiny, repeated edge.
Holding periods are short and end-of-day inventory is small: HFT firms are rarely making leveraged directional bets.
Profit per trade is tiny; profit comes from volume × edge − costs, so both scale and cost-control (latency, fees, losses) decide who wins.
It is a team sport across traders/researchers (the strategy), developers (the system), and infra/hardware (the speed).
concept.keyIdea: HFT earns a small, statistical edge an enormous number of times. Winning means being faster and more reliable than competitors while never letting a single mistake scale.

deepDive.intro: Let's make the economics concrete and see why every microsecond and every basis point of cost is fought over.

steps.title: The unit economics of a spread
steps.detail: Suppose you make a market in a stock with a 1-cent spread and you capture, on average, 0.2 cents of edge per share after adverse selection. On 100 million shares a day that is $200,000/day of gross edge from one name. Multiply across thousands of names and venues. The edge per trade is microscopic; the business is built on turnover.

steps.title: Why latency converts directly to money
steps.detail: When the market moves, there is a race to update or cancel your now-stale quote before someone picks it off, and a race to be the order that gets filled at a newly attractive price. If you are 1µs slower, you are systematically the one left holding bad fills. Latency is not vanity — it is the difference between capturing edge and donating it.

steps.title: Adverse selection: the maker's core risk
steps.detail: When someone trades against your quote, ask why. Often they know something you don't (the price is about to move their way). A market maker's profitability hinges on collecting the spread from uninformed flow faster than informed flow can pick them off. Managing this — via fast cancels, smart quoting, and signals — is the whole game.

steps.title: Costs that eat the edge
steps.detail: Exchange fees/rebates, co-location and data costs, clearing, and most of all losses from bad fills. A strategy with positive gross edge can be net-negative after costs. HFT firms obsess over fee tiers, rebate capture, and minimizing 'toxic' fills.

steps.title: Capacity and competition
steps.detail: Edges decay as competitors find them. Speed advantages get arbitraged away as everyone co-locates and buys FPGAs. So firms continuously invest in faster systems and new signals just to stay in place — a technological red-queen race.

notes.title: HFT vs. 'quant' more broadly
notes.detail: Not all quant trading is high-frequency. Stat-arb funds may hold for days; systematic macro for months. HFT specifically lives at the fast end where microstructure and latency dominate. The skills overlap, but HFT uniquely rewards low-latency systems engineering.

pitfalls: Thinking HFT 'predicts the market'. Most strategies are direction-agnostic over their horizon; they harvest structure and speed, not forecasts.
Assuming faster always wins. Speed is necessary but not sufficient — a fast system quoting bad prices just loses money faster.
Ignoring that the same code runs millions of times: a tiny logic error or unbounded position is a firm-ending event, which is why risk controls are sacred.

practice.intro: These are warm-up conceptual questions of the kind that open an HFT interview to check you actually understand the business — not just the buzzwords.

interviewQuestions.q: A market maker captures 0.3 cents of edge per share on average but trades 50 million shares a day in a name. A competitor is 2µs faster. Qualitatively, what happens to your edge and why?
a: The faster competitor wins the races that matter: they cancel stale quotes before getting picked off and they get filled first on newly attractive prices. You are left disproportionately with the 'toxic' fills — the ones that happen right before the price moves against you.

So your *average* edge per share shrinks (more adverse selection) even though the headline spread is unchanged. In the limit, your gross 0.3 cents can turn negative net of adverse selection and fees. This is exactly why firms spend enormously to shave microseconds — it's not vanity, it converts directly into realized edge.
followups: How would you quantify 'adverse selection' from your fill data?
If you can't win the speed race, what non-speed levers could preserve edge (wider quotes, better signals, different venues)?

interviewQuestions.q: Contrast how a market-making strategy and a cross-venue arbitrage strategy make money. Which carries more inventory risk?
a: Market making earns the bid-ask spread by passively providing liquidity (posting resting orders) and getting filled by others; its risk is adverse selection and the inventory it accumulates while waiting to offset.

Cross-venue arbitrage earns a (near) riskless difference by simultaneously buying the cheaper venue and selling the dearer one when the same/related instrument is mispriced; ideally both legs fill near-instantly, so inventory risk is small but execution/legging risk (one leg fills, the other doesn't) is the danger.

Market making generally carries more sustained inventory risk because it holds positions while waiting for offsetting flow; arbitrage aims to be flat almost immediately, so its dominant risk is execution/legging rather than holding.

interviewQuestions.q: Your friend says 'HFT is just predicting the market really fast.' Why is that mostly wrong?
a: Most HFT strategies are agnostic to long-term direction. A market maker profits whether the price goes up or down, as long as it collects the spread and manages inventory. An arbitrageur profits from a relative mispricing, not a directional view.

Where prediction does appear, it's over extremely short horizons (microseconds to seconds) and is statistical, not a 'view' — e.g., 'given the current order-book imbalance, the next tick is slightly more likely to be up.' The business is harvesting microstructure and being fast/reliable, not forecasting tomorrow's close.

interviewQuestions.q: Is HFT the same thing as algorithmic or quantitative trading? How do they relate?
a: No — they're overlapping but distinct. Algorithmic trading means any strategy whose orders are generated by a computer following rules; it spans horizons from microseconds to months. Quantitative trading means strategies driven by mathematical/statistical models (which may or may not be fast). HFT is a *subset* of algorithmic trading defined by speed and holding period: very short holding times, very high order/cancel rates, and latency as a primary competitive edge.

So all HFT is algorithmic, but most algorithmic/quant trading is not HFT. A multi-day statistical-arbitrage model at a quant fund is quant + algorithmic but not HFT; a microsecond market-making engine racing to the top of the book is all three. The distinguishing features of HFT are the obsession with latency/jitter, the tiny per-trade edge multiplied over enormous volume, and the infrastructure (colocation, kernel bypass, FPGAs) built to win the speed race.
followups: Does longer holding period always mean less tech?

interviewQuestions.q: If spreads are a fraction of a cent, how does an HFT firm actually make money?
a: Volume × tiny edge × high win-rate, with strict risk control. A market maker earns a fraction of the spread (or a maker rebate) on each round trip, captures it millions of times a day across many instruments, and keeps inventory near flat so it isn't betting on direction. The per-trade profit is minuscule, but the law of large numbers turns a small positive expectancy per trade into a smooth aggregate P&L — much like a casino's house edge.

Other HFT revenue: latency/statistical arbitrage (capturing fleeting price discrepancies across venues or correlated instruments before they close), and maker rebates from exchanges. The common thread is a small, repeatable, statistically-verified edge realized at huge scale and high speed, with tight per-position and aggregate risk limits so a bad streak can't wipe out the accumulated edge.
followups: Why is high win-rate plus tiny edge less risky than rare big wins?
How does inventory risk threaten this model?

problems.title: Estimate a market maker's daily revenue
problems.statement: A market maker quotes a stock and, on average, captures half the spread on each share it trades. The spread is $0.01 (so half-spread = $0.005/share). It trades 20 million shares/day on this name, but adverse selection means it loses an average of $0.003/share on the ~30% of volume that trades against it just before the price moves. Estimate gross daily revenue on this stock, and explain which assumption most threatens the estimate.
problems.hint: Split volume into 'benign' (captures half-spread) and 'adversely selected' (loses). Compute each contribution and net them.
problems.tests: EV reasoning about the market-making business model.

approach: Benign volume ≈ 70% × 20M = 14M shares earning +$0.005 each → +$70,000. Adversely-selected volume ≈ 30% × 20M = 6M shares losing $0.003 each → −$18,000 (the price moved against the maker right after the fill). Net gross ≈ $70,000 − $18,000 = $52,000/day on this single name.

Scaled across hundreds or thousands of names this becomes a meaningful business, and exchange maker rebates can add to it. The most fragile assumption is the adverse-selection rate and its cost: if better-informed (toxic) flow rises, the fraction and per-share loss on adverse fills grow, and the edge can flip negative. That's exactly why market makers widen spreads, skew quotes, and pull liquidity when flow looks toxic — managing adverse selection is the core risk of the model.

problems.title: Classify the activity
problems.statement: For each, state whether it is HFT, non-HFT algorithmic/quant, or discretionary, and justify in one line: (a) an FPGA market maker requoting in 300 ns; (b) a pension fund's VWAP execution algo working an order over a day; (c) a quant fund holding a statistical factor model for weeks; (d) a human trader clicking buy on a hunch; (e) a latency-arb bot exploiting a 50µs price lag between two exchanges.
problems.hint: Key axes: is it computer-generated (algorithmic)? model-driven (quant)? and is speed/holding-period the defining edge (HFT)?
problems.tests: Precise placement of activities on the speed/automation spectrum.

approach: (a) HFT — automated, speed is the entire edge, ultra-short horizon. (b) Non-HFT algorithmic execution — computer-driven but the goal is low-impact execution over hours, not a latency race. (c) Non-HFT quant — model-driven, automated, but multi-week holding; speed isn't the edge. (d) Discretionary — human judgment, not algorithmic. (e) HFT — automated, sub-millisecond, speed is the edge (latency arbitrage).

The point: 'algorithmic', 'quant', and 'HFT' are different axes. Automation (algorithmic), model-driven (quant), and speed-as-edge/short-horizon (HFT) can each be present or absent. HFT requires the speed/short-horizon axis specifically.

problems.title: Why latency is an edge: a concrete race
problems.statement: Two market makers, A and B, both want to post the new best bid after a favorable news tick. A's tick-to-trade is 1µs; B's is 5µs. The exchange uses price-time priority and there's room for only a limited quantity at the front of the queue. Explain, step by step, what happens and why A's 4µs advantage translates into profit — and what B might do instead of trying to win the speed race.
problems.hint: Think about queue position under price-time priority and who gets filled by the next incoming order.
problems.tests: Connecting latency to queue priority and economic outcome.

approach: When the triggering event hits, A reacts in 1µs and posts its order first, claiming the front of the queue at the new best price. B arrives 4µs later and lands behind A. Under price-time priority, the next incoming aggressive order fills A first; A captures the spread/rebate and the favorable fill, while B's order may never trade at that price (the market moves) or trades only after A is done. So A's latency edge converts directly into queue priority, which converts into fills, which converts into P&L. Repeated millions of times, that 4µs is the difference between a profitable and an unprofitable book.

If B can't win the pure speed race, it competes differently: post at prices A isn't contesting, use better signals to quote only when edge is high (smarter, not just faster), capture rebates, provide liquidity in less-contested names, or specialize where its latency is sufficient. Not everyone can be the fastest, so most firms combine 'fast enough' infrastructure with superior signals and risk management.
